text:
Court of Queen’s Bench of Alberta

Citation: R v Smith-Lowe, 2022 ABQB 494

Date:
20220715

Docket:
211043088U3

Registry:
Calgary

Between:

Her Majesty the Queen

Crown

- and -

Tyler Smith-Lowe

Accused

_______________________________________________________

Decision

of the

Honourable Mr. Justice

N.E. Devlin

_______________________________________________________

[
1
]

Tyler Smith-Lowe applies for judicial interim release on a series of charges for which he is presently detained by the order of Judge Fradsham. He brings this bail review pursuant to
section 521
of the
Criminal Code
, arguing that there has been a change in circumstances and he is now releasable on a revised plan. The Crown opposes his release on primary, secondary and, I infer, tertiary grounds, and also argues that there has not been a sufficient change in circumstances to warrant a review as required by the Supreme Court’s guidance in
R v St-Cloud
,
2015 SCC 328
.

The Outstanding Charges

[
2
]

Mr. Smith-Lowe faces many charges. For simplicity, they can be considered in roughly four groupings.

The Residential Break and Enters

[
3
]

The first set of charges for which release is sought relate to a series of residential B&Es that took place in Calgary between January and February of 2021. The Crown alleges that these followed a pattern wherein three individuals, one of them allegedly the accused, would approach a home that was unoccupied by virtue of the homeowner being absent during the pandemic. The homes would be broken into, ransacked, valuables stolen, and on some occasion’s vehicles taken.

[
4
]

The case against the accused in respect of these crimes consists primarily of the statement and anticipated evidence of one of his co-conspirators, a woman who was seen participating in the robberies. She has pled guilty and implicated Mr. Smith-Lowe directly as a co-actor in these crimes.

[
5
]

Mr. Smith-Lowe’s fingerprint was found on the steering wheel of a vehicle stolen from one of the burgled residences. That home was broken into between January 12th, 13th, and 14th, 2021. The intruders stole a 2019 Mercedes-Benz E53 AMG, a high-end vehicle, and fled the home in it. The vehicle was seen shortly thereafter speeding on 16th Avenue Northeast.

[
6
]

Police pulled the vehicle over and realized that it was registered to an Asian lady, not the individual driving. It appears that the vehicle fled from police during the stop. Police subsequently tracked it through a built-in GPS system. Using that technology, police found the Mercedes within the hour parked in an empty carwash in the northeast. The Mercedes was seen in the company of a red F-350 that was stolen from another one of the residences Mr. Smith-Lowe is charged with burgling. The police followed the two vehicles, though apparently not particularly closely, as they were ultimately found abandoned at an address in the northeast. The Mercedes was seized and towed. Mr. Smith-Lowe’s fingerprint was found allegedly on the steering wheel.

[
7
]

Mr. Smith-Lowe was arrested on a warrant-in-the-first on these offences as he was not residing at the location specified in a Conditional Sentence Order imposed earlier in January. He was released on these charges on a form 11.

The ‘Overdose Charges’

[
8
]

On June 1st, 2021, at 9:30 in the morning, a woman called police saying she believed a man was overdosing from drugs. That man was Mr. Smith-Lowe. He was found in a vehicle belonging to someone else. He told the police he was Ryan Jenkins. That name comes to matter later on. He had a lot of cash in his pockets. Police searched the vehicle and found a black bag inside. The bag contained a replica handgun and a cornucopia of drugs, including two forms of methamphetamine, cocaine, MDMA, and marijuana. Police tell Mr. Smith-Lowe that they know he is not who he says he is and caution him about being further charged with obstruction. He provides another false name.

[
9
]

It turns out the car he is in was stolen during a break and enter from a family home that was left vacant due to the occupants being stranded outside the country during COVID. In the final tally, police find over $3,100, multiple SIM cards, empty baggies, the drugs, and a bag containing pry bars and other miscellaneous tools in the vehicle. These did not belong to the vehicle’s rightful owner. Mr. Smith-Lowe was released again on a form 11.

The Drug Charges

[
10
]

In September 2021, Mr. Smith-Lowe and Cassandra St. Onge were charged with two counts of possessing cocaine and methamphetamine. I have relatively little information about these charges but have been advised that they have, since the bail hearing before Judge Fradsham, been upped to two counts of possession for the purpose of trafficking, contrary to section 5(2) of the CDSA. I heard that Ms. St. Onge is the accused’s common-law partner. Her mother, Carol, is offered as the surety on this application and is proposing that Mr. Smith-Lowe live with the St. Onges in a residence just outside Calgary. I will deal more with this in due course.

[
11
]

I have little information regarding the strength of the drug charges against Mr. Smith-Lowe. He was again granted release.

The Grossman Counts

[
12
]

The final broad category of charges against Mr. Smith-Lowe relate to a series of events commencing October 21, 2021. On that day, the home of an older Jewish couple was burgled while they were away in Vancouver. On October 24th, Mr. Grossman - the homeowner - received a call from a number that displayed on his phone as ending in ‘1568’. The person on the other end of the line said his name was Ryan Jenkins. He made conversation in respect of non-profit work that Mr. Grossman is involved with, in the course of which it was confirmed that the Grossmans were out of town.

[
13
]

About an hour later another call came in from the same number, from the same voice, except this time the person started to threaten the Grossmans using antisemitic slurs and comments about the Jewish community. The comments were crass and vile and ended with a demand for $1,000,000 and kilos of gold. The demands were backed with a threat that, if they are not met, the caller “would not say what would happen to the Grossmans and their little gross people”. A further series of text messages came to the Grossman’s phone from the same 1568 number. They contained similar degrading antisemitic statements.

[
14
]

Around the time the phone calls and texts were happening, a neighbour saw a person coming in and out of the Grossman’s home taking large paintings. She then saw that person leave in the Grossman’s Porsche 911. That neighbour called the Grossman’s daughter and told her what was happening. A few hours later, the Porsche was located by Calgary Police and followed by ground units and HAWCS helicopter to a liquor store on 16th Avenue. Mr. Smith-Lowe exited the driver’s seat and entered the liquor store. When he left and was arrested, he gave another false name. He was the only occupant of the stolen Porsche.

[
15
]

Police searched the Porsche incident to arrest and found two cell phones. One of the officers investigating the extortion calls made to the Grossmans learned of the accused’s arrest and called the 1568 phone. One of the phones found in the Porsche rang. It was the 1568 phone.

The Previous Detention Order

[
16
]

A bail hearing was heard before Judge Fradsham on two dates in late November and early December 2021. In his reasons declining to release Mr. Smith-Lowe, Judge Fradsham noted the repeated pattern of release and re-charge. He observed that despite being at least three release orders deep by October 24th, Mr. Smith-Lowe was found in the Grossman’s stolen vehicle. He found that the concerns arising from these facts were not assuaged by the presentation of two sureties, one of whom was the younger Ms. St. Onge, his co-accused on the drug charges.

[
17
]

The other surety, a young lady named Ms. Wall, was found to be well-meaning but lacking insight in the ability to control the accused. For those reasons, Judge Fradsham found that Mr. Smith-Lowe had not met his onus to show cause that he should be granted bail.

Change in Circumstances

[
18
]

While an accused person may bring a bail review at any time, the Supreme Court in
St-Cloud

made clear that an application should not be granted unless the previous detention order was the result of an error or a material change in circumstance had been shown.

[
19
]

In this case, the defence asserts two changes in circumstance. The first is that Mr. Smith-Lowe has recently been acquitted of a series of charges involving dangerous driving that were still outstanding at the time of Judge Fradsham’s ruling. These predated his January 2021 conditional sentence order.

[
20
]

The second development the applicant relies on is a change in the release plan. The elder Ms. St. Onge is now proposed as a live-in surety and Mr. Smith-Lowe has offered to wear an electronic ankle monitoring bracelet provided by Recovery Science.

[
21
]

The Crown urges me to find that this is not really a change in circumstances. It argues that a different or better surety is insufficient to allow a fresh bail review. The Crown further argues that Mr. Smith-Lowe’s acquittal is offset by the fact that his drug charges have been elevated from simple possession to possession for the purposes of trafficking, yielding a net increase in the severity and jeopardy on the charges he faces.

[
22
]

I begin by observing that there is no suggestion that Judge Fradsham’s ruling was wrong. However, I am satisfied that a change in circumstances sufficient to warrant a review has been made out. The constitutionally guaranteed right to reasonable bail is a continuing right secured by section 11(e) of the
Charter
. In a reverse onus situation such as this, an accused person has the right to be released from custody if and when they satisfy the Court that terms exist which ameliorate the primary, secondary, and tertiary ground concerns underlying their detention.

[
23
]

This right necessarily comprises the opportunity to persuade a Court that an answer is offered for those concerns which underwrote their previous detention. Repeated bail applications in largely unchanged circumstances are self-evidently an abuse of process. The reviewing Court must not sit in indefinite appeal of itself on a more or less identical bail application. However, where an accused person has provided a new and different release plan in an attempt to answer the Court’s previously articulated concerns, he or she should be heard.

[
24
]

In this case, while Mr. Smith-Lowe continues to propose living with his co-accused on the drug charges, he offers a new and more suitable surety, and at least partial residential supervision by that surety in combination with electronic monitoring. That package constitutes a change in circumstance sufficient to permit this Court to undertake a fresh bail analysis.

Releases and Criminal History

[
25
]

Two factors on any bail application are whether the accused was already on forms of judicial release when the charges before the Court arose and their criminal record. Both factors figure prominently in this case. At the time of the initial B&Es in January and February of 2021, Mr. Smith-Lowe was serving a four-month conditional sentence that had been imposed in early January. He was also on release for the dangerous driving episode of which he was subsequently acquitted. As mentioned, when police went to arrest him on the B&Es, he became the subject of a warrant in the first as he was not resident where required under the conditional sentence.

[
26
]

At the time of each of the subsequent sequential allegations, he was on judicial interim release for all the previous ones. He was three or four releases deep by the time the Grossman allegations arose. I say three or four because the disposition of the conditional sentence order is unclear on the record before me. This places him in a reverse onus situation on all of the charges.

[
27
]

Mr. Smith-Lowe also has a prodigious criminal record. It contains a total of 40 entries running in a mostly unbroken string since 2004. Three of those convictions are for break and enter: in 2004 as a youth and twice in 2018. The 2018 convictions resulted in a sentence of 15 months in light of just over a month of pre-sentence custody on each of the two counts.

[
28
]

Mr. Smith-Lowe has been convicted of obstruction four times, as well as personation with intent. He has 14 convictions for failure to comply with release conditions or failure to attend court. He was incarcerated as a parole violator on his first federal sentence in 2010 and has a conviction for being unlawfully at large.

[
29
]

He has been convicted of driving while disqualified on five occasions and twice for dangerous driving. On the first dangerous driving conviction, he received the equivalent of a 43-month penitentiary term, speaking to the gravity of the offence. Finally, he has multiple counts of theft and possession of property obtained by crime on his record.

[
30
]

Mr. Smith-Lowe’s criminal antecedents give rise to primary and particularly serious secondary grounds concerns. Consistent with the evidence I heard that Mr. Smith-Lowe has a longstanding problem with addiction, his criminal record looks like that of an addict. Unfortunately, it is the record of an addict who is dangerous and ungovernable when in the clutches of his drug. His criminal record demonstrates that court-imposed conditions have no meaning or impact for him.

[
31
]

Of equal concern, the present array of charges repeats many patterns seen from Mr. Smith-Lowe’s past; home burglaries, large-scale theft, and the persistent obstruction of police through the use of false names.

The Proposed Surety

[
32
]

Ms. Carol St. Onge was presented by the defence and testified about why she was willing to step forward for Mr. Smith-Lowe and how she was willing to supervise him. She was cross-examined by the Crown on her knowledge of the circumstances in which she proposed to live with the accused, as well as the depth and nature of her understanding of the charges he faces.

[
33
]

While the examination of sureties before bail courts is common practice in many jurisdictions, that is less the case in Alberta. With the move away from cash bails pursuant to the guidance of the Supreme Court in
R v Antic
,
2017 SCC 27
, the practice of examining and cross-examining proposed sureties should become more commonplace here. Sureties are a far superior form of release to cash in that they provide a prosocial influence to the accused individuals, as well as a continuous set of supervising eyes in the community. In turn, hearing from sureties personally is often revelatory as to their suitability. Some sureties significantly impress the Court with their clarity, candour, and strength of character such that a release to them as the gaoler in the community becomes a viable answer to significant primary, secondary, and even tertiary grounds which would otherwise see an accused person detained.

[
34
]

On the other hand, even a brief examination may reveal a surety to be underinformed, naïve, or otherwise unprepared for the task of supervising someone with potentially significant criminal involvement. I strongly urge counsel in the Provincial Court, in which bail applications are most often heard, to adopt the practice of presenting and examining sureties in serious cases. Public safety and confidence in the administration of justice will be greatly enhanced if this is done.

[
35
]

In this case, the proposed surety release plan is that Ms. St. Onge move in with her daughter Cassandra and the accused in a five-bedroom home that her daughter rents with a roommate in Balzac, Alberta. She offers a non-deposit surety pledge of $2,500. While Ms. St. Onge said she planned to come back to Calgary regularly for work during the day, she otherwise proposed to live full-time with her daughter and the accused.

[
36
]

I wish to state from the outset that Mr. Smith-Lowe is very lucky to have someone such as Ms. St. Onge step up for him. She testified that she is doing so because of her daughter’s connection with him and her own fondness for him arising over the 15 years she has known him. She testified that he is “non-violent” and is kind, sweet, giving, and a hard worker. She testified that her daughter Cassandra is now 31 years old and a drug treatment court graduate. She told the Court that she and Cassandra had not lived together since her daughter was a teen. She believes her daughter had lived in Balzac with her roommate Juanita for some time but did not know Juanita’s last name.

[
37
]

Ms. St. Onge was very candid in saying she thinks Cassandra might be using again. She did not know what her daughter was doing for a living to pay for her share of the rent, nor indeed how much the rent at this house was. She had previously driven past the house but never attended there until the weekend before the bail hearing. Ms. St. Onge testified that this was the last chance for both Mr. Smith-Lowe and her daughter. She was clear that she would pull the bail if she believed they were using drugs again. To her benefit as a potential surety in this case, Ms. St. Onge has a lifetime of experience with the scourge of addiction and its impact on family members. She is not naïve about what drugs do to people and knows the signs of active addiction.

[
38
]

Ms. St. Onge was aware of the charges against the accused but expressed the view that the police perhaps did not have this right and she thinks Mr. Smith-Lowe was not the person who committed the alleged offences. Sureties will often be loved ones and family members who may well side with an accused person who asserts their innocence. This in no way disqualifies them from acting as a surety.

[
39
]

In this case, however, I did find that Ms. St. Onge downplayed the gravity of the situation somewhat. In cross-examination, she agreed that the police had attended multiple times at the Balzac property in recent months, including a visit by a tactical team to remove Juanita’s ex-husband. She was critical of the police for smashing windows during this event. Ms. St. Onge was also aware the police had attended to recover a stolen vehicle left at the property by others. A printout of police contact with the Balzac residence at which Mr. Smith-Lowe is supposed to live was admitted as further evidence. It is clear that the police have attended numerous times in addition to the occasions referenced by Ms. St. Onge.

Electronic Monitoring

[
40
]

In addition to the proposed surety, the defence provided a copy of the partially completed contract between Mr. Smith-Lowe and Recovery Sciences, a company which provides continuous ankle monitoring. The courts are familiar with this service and it often provides an independent check that enhances the security afforded by a house arrest bail. I would note that there is a cautionary caveat in Recovery Science’s materials indicating that they have some difficulty integrating permission letters from provincial probation authorities in Alberta that may somewhat undercut the effectiveness of their service.

A Further Offer of Cash Deposit

[
41
]

In addition to the surety and ankle monitoring, Mr. Smith-Lowe offers to deposit 5,000 cash. This offer is in keeping with a continuing practice in this province to mix cash with surety bails for accused ordinarily resident in the jurisdiction. I do not fault counsel for advancing this offer of increased bail but it is not a legal one. Section 515(2) permits cash on top of surety bail only in the case of a non-resident accused. Indeed, the bail court having insisted on this form of enhanced deposit of cash was the very legal error identified at the heart of the Supreme Court’s decision in
Antic
.

[
42
]

I do not consider this offer of cash as part of the bail plan.

[
43
]

As I stated in court, in a case like this the real question is the suitability of the surety and the plan of supervision. I would not deny Mr. Smith-Lowe bail for want of the additional cash. Conversely, to be blunt, if a good surety is not enough to meet an accused person’s onus to be released, that is a sign that he or she is not releasable. Where the Court is not satisfied that an accused can be safety and successfully released into the community with a strong surety, they do not become more releasable for a few dollars more.

Guiding Principles

[
44
]

The accused is in a reverse onus position and must satisfy the Court that he has shown cause to be released. Detention is the default state and the onus lies on him to prove release is appropriate: section 515(6).

[
45
]

Parenthetically, nothing about the Supreme Court’s leading decision in
R v Antic
changes this. I am aware that it has been suggested in various quarters that the ladder principle must be applied in reverse onus cases. This is incorrect and reflects a misunderstanding of that principle. As Justice Trotter observed in his seminal treatise,
The Law of Bail in Canada
, 3rd ed. Toronto: Carswell, 2010 (loose-leaf updated 2019, release 1):
“The ladder principle is inapplicable in situations in which a reverse onus provision in section 515(6) is triggered”.

[
46
]

That said, an analogue to the ladder principle does exist and should be observed in reverse onus situations. Specifically, the accused person’s right to reasonable bail means that they are entitled to the least onerous form of release which ameliorates the primary, secondary, and tertiary concerns standing between them and judicial interim release in their specific case.

[
47
]

On the other hand, neither the recently reformed bail provisions of the
Criminal Code
, nor the Supreme Court’s decision in
Antic

stipulate that every accused person is, in fact, suitable for bail. There will be instances in which concerns over the accused’s attendance at court, risk to commit further offences, and the general impact of their release on community confidence in the administration of justice will be such that even a very strong bail plan is not sufficient for them to meet their onus to be released.

Application of the Principles to This Case

[
48
]

The charges against Mr. Smith-Lowe are all serious. He is alleged to have committed all of them while in the community on some form of judicial release. These crimes are all consistent with an addict in the throes of drug involvement. While that fact engenders sympathy for the addicted person, that sympathy does not offset the fact that Mr. Smith-Lowe is alleged to have visited the impact of his addiction on many innocent members of the community in damaging ways.

[
49
]

That said, the strength of these charges is variable. The B&E counts rely on a
Vetrovec
witness and a few points of circumstantial connection. The case against Mr. Smith-Lowe on the occasion of his overdose seems somewhat stronger, though the charges are less serious. However, those counts also rely on circumstantial inferences of possession. Judicial experience tells us that such cases are not invariably successful. I have little information as to the details of the drug counts, diminishing the hurdle Mr. Smith-Lowe must overcome in respect of those charges. The problem posed by those charges is that they suggest that conduct occurred involving him and the lady he has proposed to live with that is directly connected to intense drug activity.

[
50
]

The Grossman counts are another matter. Mr. Smith-Lowe’s connection to the Porsche is temporally proximate to its departure from the Grossman residence, at which time a witness saw it as being removed from the home, and which may be shown to have been contemporaneous with the calls to Mr. Grossman. Moreover, the use of the name “Ryan Jenkins” in the call to Mr. Grossman is a significant fact which, if Mr. Smith-Lowe’s previous use of that false name is also proven, give rise to a strong inference that he was the caller. The presence of the phone from which the exceptionally vile extortion calls were made in the Grossman’s stolen car, which Mr. Smith-Lowe was driving by himself, elevate these charges to a significant level of strength.

[
51
]

While this set of counts is also circumstantial to some extent, it seems to be the strongest and most serious set of allegations. Breaking into someone’s home and stealing their most prized possessions is, in itself, a major violation. Extorting money under threat through knowledge of the details of the victim’s personal life is even worse. The addition of the disgusting antisemitic comments and threats with which the extortion was flavoured elevate these already serious offences to the level of a hate crime.

[
52
]

While I fully appreciate that Mr. Smith-Lowe is presumed innocent of these charges and may successfully defend them, the more closely the Crown’s proffered evidence connects him to these events, the more he looks like an individual who lacks moral bounds whenever he is seeking money to fuel his addiction.

[
53
]

In the case before me, that connection is strong enough to both elevate the secondary ground concerns to their highest level and bring tertiary grounds into play. The idea that someone already on multiple layers of judicial release would abuse and terrorize members of the community in this manner for money and be further released would rightly give the public concern as to whether their safety is being adequately protected.

[
54
]

In summary, there is a very significant chance of reoffence in this case if Mr. Smith-Lowe reconnects with his drug use in any way. Both his record and the allegations before me suggest that such a reoffence would come at a significant cost to other innocent members of the public. I think that risk to be both significant and intolerable.

[
55
]

These concerns and risks are not sufficiently mitigated by the release plan in this case. While a much better surety than previously proposed, Ms. St. Onge wears rose-coloured glasses where this accused is concerned. She describes him as non-violent. His criminal record unfortunately suggests otherwise. While he has not committed assaults, which is significantly to his credit, one does not receive a four-year penitentiary term for dangerous driving without committing significant acts of physical violence. Moreover, the act of breaking into a dwelling house by force is, itself, violent as is the carrying of imitation firearms, as alleged in this case.

[
56
]

I do not criticize Ms. St. Onge for the faith she showed in Mr. Smith-Lowe. I find that she does not fully appreciate what she would be walking into. She suspects but does not know if her daughter is using, does not know what she does for a living, and does not know how the rent is paid at her house. Ms. St. Onge does not know anything about the roommate other than that her ex is a violent criminal, apparently.

[
57
]

She does, however, fear that her daughter is using again. This tells me first that she is unsure of her daughter’s condition. Second, it indicates there is a risk of the presence of a drug influence in the home where Mr. Smith-Lowe is proposed to live. It appears there is a possibility that his intimate partner remains in the grasp of addiction, and, as such, would most likely drag him back down into the same hole no matter how good his intentions.

[
58
]

The Balzac house is a manifestly unsatisfactory venue of release. It is obviously a significant problem location at which repeated police attendance has been necessary. It is the last kind of place Mr. Smith-Lowe needs to be and seems like the exact sort of place he will reconnect with the criminal subculture. Respectfully, Ms. St. Onge seems a bit too resigned to the presence of addiction and a criminal element as a chronic part of her life. She may be both too kind and too lenient to rule the roost sufficiently in a milieu such as this.

[
59
]

Neither the surety who has pledged to phone the police if trouble occurs, nor the presence of an electronic ankle monitoring bracelet prevent Mr. Smith-Lowe from simply leaving the residence and going about his business in the community. Unfortunately, his criminal record describes a willingness to do this. I have considered the case law regarding the use of electronic monitoring, including circumstances where there are significant secondary and even tertiary grounds concerns. This is a helpful technology which will often provide the necessary comfort on house arrest bail. However, electronic monitoring is not a panacea for an accused whose risk of reoffence and dangerousness make them otherwise unreleasable and where the foreseen magnitude of any reoffence is too grave.

[
60
]

I find that this is such a case. Simply put, the harm that would be done to the community and to the repute of the administration of justice were Mr. Smith-Lowe to walk away from the monitoring in pursuit of further drug endeavours is not tolerable. A removed bracelet would neither recapture him, nor prevent the further offences which would likely follow.

[
61
]

I appreciate that Mr. Smith-Lowe’s trial on all of these matters are imminent. While this lowers the impact that a continue detention order will have on his liberty interests, I appreciate that it would be much easier for him to prepare for trial out of custody. That weighed heavily on my consideration of tertiary grounds. It also creates a situation, however, where he may well be in a position to revisit the question of bail if he is successful in defending some of these charges before trial judges who will have a better sense of the strength of the evidence and his circumstances.

[
62
]

For the moment, however, there remains an overwhelming and uncontrolled risk that Mr. Smith-Lowe will continue with a course of conduct that injures members of the community significantly, despite what I take to be his best intentions. Notwithstanding Mr. Zuk’s hard work in assembling this plan of release and very able advocacy on behalf of his client, Mr. Smith-Lowe has not satisfied this Court that it is safe to release him and he will remain detained pending trial.

[
63
]

And I am sorry that result is disappointing to some of those here today but it is the one that my application of the law compelled.

Heard on the
6
th
day of May, 2022.

Dated
at the City of Calgary, Alberta this
15
th
day of July, 2022.

N.E. Devlin

J.C.Q.B.A.

Appearances:

Donna Spaner

for the Crown

Dean Zuk
